sources.title: S. M. Carroll, Lecture Notes on General Relativity, arXiv:gr-qc/9712019v1 (December 1997), Ch. 8 'Cosmology'

contents.name: Ch. 8 p. 217: the Copernican principle and its observational motivation on the largest scales
contents.support: The adopted model postulate states the homogeneity-and-isotropy idealization and its scope; the source's observational motivation is recorded as motivation only, not as a derivation.

contents.name: Ch. 8 pp. 217-218: isotropy and homogeneity as mathematical properties of a manifold
contents.support: The spatial model datum turns the local curvature condition into a precise mathematical hypothesis and explicitly disclaims any classification or global-isotropy theorem.

contents.name: Ch. 8 (8.1)-(8.7) pp. 218-219: the maximally symmetric three-metric, the Robertson-Walker metric with k = -1,0,+1 and the scale factor
contents.support: The FLRW model datum is defined with these exact ingredients: time interval, constant-curvature spatial model, scale factor, metric and comoving congruence.

contents.name: Ch. 8 (8.2)-(8.3) pp. 218-219: the curvature of the maximally symmetric three-spaces, (3)R_ijkl = k(gamma_ik gamma_jl - gamma_il gamma_jk) and (3)R_jl = 2k gamma_jl
contents.support: The lemma proves the dimension-three equivalence between constant sectional curvature, the tensor identity and the Ricci condition Ric = 2k gamma used by the spatial model definition.

contents.name: Ch. 8 pp. 219-223: connection coefficients, Ricci and Einstein tensors of the Robertson-Walker metric
contents.support: The lemma's proof recomputes the symbols and the Ricci, scalar and Einstein components in product charts with explicit dimensions; the source's component list is absorbed there.

contents.name: Ch. 8 p. 219: the normalisation of the spatial curvature to k = -1,0,+1 and the reading of the scale factor as the size of the spatial slices
contents.support: The lemma proves that a constant rescaling of the spatial metric preserves the connection, Ricci tensor and sectional curvatures, which is the invariance that makes the three-sign normalisation and the scale-factor reading of the spatial geometry well posed.

contents.name: Ch. 8 (8.9)-(8.15) pp. 220-221: the perfect-fluid stress-energy tensor in the comoving frame
contents.support: The theorem's stress-energy step displays T_00 = epsilon c^2, T_0i = 0 and T_ij = p a^2 gamma_ij for the comoving fluid, which is what the reduced components use.

contents.name: Ch. 8 (8.20)-(8.23) pp. 221-222: the equation of state p = w rho and the continuity equation
contents.support: The proposition differentiates the Friedmann equation and substitutes the continuity equation, with the H = 0 caveat; the source's continuity equation is used in that form.

contents.name: Ch. 8 (8.32)-(8.37) pp. 222-223: the 00 and ij Einstein equations, the Friedmann equations and H = a-dot/a
contents.support: The Friedmann-system datum is defined by exactly these equations, with the dimensions of each term stated and no equation of state adopted by the definition.

contents.name: Ch. 8 (8.38)-(8.46) pp. 223-225: critical density, Omega parameters and the flatness reading
contents.reason: Density parameters and the flatness reading require measured densities and a data-comparison interface; this batch asserts no observed value, and the observational architecture belongs to the later experimental-interface page of the run.

contents.name: Ch. 8 (8.47)-(8.53) pp. 225-227: single-component solutions and the flat dust and radiation power laws
contents.support: The theorem verifies the flat barotropic power-law data against the reduced equations and derives the density scaling, with the dust and radiation exponents recorded.

contents.name: Ch. 8 (8.54)-(8.59) p. 227: the flat vacuum models and the sign condition Lambda > 0 with a proportional to exp(+/- sqrt(Lambda/3) t)
contents.support: The theorem verifies the exponential datum for Lambda > 0 and proves the impossibility of any flat vacuum solution for Lambda < 0 by the sign of the Friedmann equation.

contents.name: Ch. 8 (8.61)-(8.67) pp. 228-229: conserved quantities along geodesics, the frequency ratio omega_0/omega_1 = a_1/a_0 and z = a_0/a_1 - 1
contents.support: The theorem proves a V^t constant along every future null geodesic and derives the observer-energy ratio and the redshift parameter relation.

contents.name: Ch. 8 (8.68) p. 229: the luminosity distance
contents.reason: Distance measures are defined from measured fluxes and luminosities with a source model and selection assumptions; the experimental-interface page of this run owns that apparatus and analysis architecture.

sources.title: D. Tong, General Relativity (Cambridge Part III Mathematical Tripos, Michaelmas 2019), section 4.6 'A Taste of Cosmology'
sources.locator: Section 4.6 'A Taste of Cosmology', sections 4.6.1-4.6.2 with the dust and radiation solutions, printed pp. 198-203 (PDF pp. 205-210).

contents.name: Sec. 4.6.1 pp. 198-199: observed homogeneity and isotropy; the FRW metric (4.63) and the comoving frame
contents.support: The adopted model postulate fixes the FLRW geometry, its comoving congruence and the physical idealization, with the observed motivation recorded as motivation only.

contents.name: Sec. 4.6.1 pp. 199-200: the three constant-curvature spatial metrics S^3, R^3 and H^3 (4.64)
contents.support: The definition names exactly these three standard complete simply connected models with k = +1, 0, -1 and proves no classification theorem.

contents.name: Sec. 4.6.1 pp. 199-200: the scale factor as the size of the spatial slices; the comoving frame and its proper-time reading
contents.support: The lemma proves that the FLRW metric is smooth Lorentzian, that the comoving curves are unit-speed observers whose parameter is proper time up to a constant, and that the slices carry the scaled spatial metric.

contents.name: Sec. 4.6.1 pp. 200-201: Christoffel symbols and the Ricci and Einstein tensors of the FRW metric
contents.support: The lemma computes the same nonvanishing symbols in product charts, with the c-dependence carried explicitly.

contents.name: Sec. 4.6.2 pp. 201-202: the perfect fluid at rest in the FRW frame, the continuity equation and the divergence of the comoving four-velocity
contents.support: The lemma computes the expansion of the comoving congruence and its divergence, the exact quantity the source evaluates for u^mu = (1,0,0,0).

contents.name: Sec. 4.6.2 pp. 202-203: the Friedmann equation (4.66), the acceleration equation (4.67) and the dust and radiation exponents
contents.support: The Friedmann-system datum collects these equations with restored dimensions and states them as pure relations among the model data.

sources.title: D. Tong, Cosmology (Cambridge Part III Mathematical Tripos, 2019 revision)

contents.name: Sec. 1.1.1 pp. 7-9: homogeneous and isotropic spaces and the three constant-curvature three-spaces (1.1)-(1.11)
contents.support: The definition adopts the same three models through the Ricci condition Ric = 2k gamma and makes the local form the mathematical hypothesis.

contents.name: Sec. 1.1.2 pp. 10-12: the FRW metric (1.12)-(1.13) and the comoving coordinates (1.14)-(1.15)
contents.support: The FLRW model datum and its comoving congruence are defined in these coordinates, with the physical readings deferred to the postulates.

contents.name: Sec. 1.1.3 pp. 13-15: redshift (1.17)-(1.23), its difference from the Doppler effect, and the identification of z through spectral features
contents.support: The theorem derives the redshift relation from the metric and the light-ray rule, and the scope note records that identifying z with a measured spectral shift needs an apparatus model.

contents.name: Sec. 1.1.4 pp. 15-16: the Big Bang and cosmological horizons
contents.reason: Horizon and initial-singularity statements require the causal and initial-value machinery owned by the later causal-boundaries page; this page asserts no horizon claim and the design defers those topics.

contents.name: Sec. 1.2.1 pp. 24-26: perfect fluids, the stress tensor (1.33)-(1.36) and the equation of state P = w rho
contents.support: The postulate adopts the comoving perfect-fluid sector with homogeneous density and pressure and an explicit equation of state, citing the fluid model of the framework's matter page.

contents.name: Sec. 1.2.2 pp. 27-28: the continuity equation (1.39)
contents.support: The continuity equation is one of the four defining equations of the Friedmann-system datum.

contents.name: Sec. 1.2.3 pp. 29-30: the Friedmann equation (1.42) with c restored
contents.support: The Friedmann equation is defined with the c^2 factors carried explicitly, so the source's c = 1 display is restored to the framework's units.

contents.name: Sec. 1.3.1 pp. 32-34: simple solutions and the Einstein-de Sitter universe
contents.support: The theorem verifies the flat power-law solutions, including the matter-dominated a proportional to t^{2/3} case.

contents.name: Sec. 1.3.3 pp. 40-43: the cosmological constant; de Sitter space
contents.support: The theorem verifies the flat vacuum exponential solution for Lambda > 0 and the sign obstruction for Lambda < 0.

contents.name: Sec. 1.3.3 p. 43: anti-de Sitter space and its negative cosmological constant
contents.reason: The negative-cosmological-constant anti-de Sitter geometry is not adopted by the homogeneous model of this page, whose flat vacuum sector is proved to admit no solution for Lambda < 0.

sources.title: H. S. Reall, Part III General Relativity (Cambridge, October 12, 2022 revision), section 6.4 'Einstein's equation'

contents.name: Postulate 4 and equation (6.32) p. 67: the Einstein equation G_ab = 8 pi G T_ab
contents.reason: The field law is adopted as the postulate of the earlier Einstein-and-matter page of this run; the present batch uses it only as the physical assumption of the reduction theorem.

contents.name: Postulate 3 p. 67: conservation of the stress-energy tensor adopted as a separate postulate
contents.reason: This framework derives conservation from the field law and the contracted Bianchi identity on the earlier page instead of adopting it; the difference from the source is recorded there.

contents.name: Postulate 2 p. 67: free particles follow geodesics
contents.reason: The free-fall and light-ray assumptions are adopted on the connections-and-free-fall page of this run; the redshift theorem consumes only its stated light-ray clause.

contents.name: The Lovelock uniqueness theorem (6.34) p. 68
contents.reason: Proving uniqueness of the Einstein tensor among divergence-free symmetric tensors needs the naturality and tensor-calculus machinery of the Lovelock theorem; this page adopts the field law without claiming uniqueness.

contents.name: The cosmological constant (6.35), its dark-energy reading and the length scale |Lambda|^{-1/2} pp. 67-68
contents.support: The theorem treats Lambda as a real model parameter entering the Friedmann system, with the positive and negative sign regimes analysed and the dark-energy interpretation left to the scope note.

contents.name: The Newtonian-limit remark p. 68
contents.reason: The weak-field and slow-motion correspondence is developed on the flat-and-Newtonian-bridges page of this run; this batch asserts no Newtonian limit of its solutions.

canonical.name: The scope and empirical status of the homogeneous cosmological model: model predictions, reported observations and statistical inference are distinct
canonical.support: The scope note records that every result of the page is conditional on the adopted model, distinguishes model quantities from apparatus-dependent records and statistical inference, and lists the idealizations the model does not capture.

sources.title: S. M. Carroll, Lecture Notes on General Relativity, arXiv:gr-qc/9712019v1 (December 1997), Ch. 8 (8.20)-(8.23) and (8.47)-(8.67)

contents.name: Ch. 8 (8.49) and (8.53) pp. 226-227: the flat dust and radiation power laws
contents.support: The example verifies the power-law data with exponent q = 2/(3(1+w)) in all four equations of the Friedmann-system definition, covering the dust and radiation cases by substitution.

contents.name: Ch. 8 (8.58) p. 227: the flat vacuum model with Lambda > 0 and the excluded Lambda < 0 case
contents.support: The example verifies the exponential datum against all four equations directly and proves the square-sign obstruction for negative Lambda.

contents.name: Ch. 8 (8.61)-(8.67) pp. 228-229: the conserved time component and the redshift ratio along null geodesics
contents.support: The example computes an explicit radial null geodesic, verifies a V^t is constant and checks the observer-energy ratio in coordinates.

sources.title: D. Tong, General Relativity (Cambridge Part III Mathematical Tripos, Michaelmas 2019), section 4.6.2
sources.locator: Section 4.6.2 with the flat single-component solutions, printed pp. 202-203 (PDF pp. 209-210).

contents.name: Sec. 4.6.2 p. 202: the comoving fluid frame u^mu = (1,0,0,0) and the continuity equation
contents.support: The example's data use a comoving perfect fluid with p = w epsilon and the continuity equation; the verification differentiates the data directly and absorbs the source's continuity relation.

contents.name: Sec. 4.6.2 pp. 202-203: the flat solutions a proportional to t^{2/3} and t^{1/2}
contents.support: The example verifies the same power-law family for arbitrary w > -1 at the level of the defining equations.

sources.title: D. Tong, Cosmology (Cambridge Part III Mathematical Tripos, 2019 revision), section 1.3.3
sources.locator: Section 1.3.3 on the cosmological constant and de Sitter space, printed pp. 40-43 (PDF pp. 46-49).

contents.name: Sec. 1.3.3 pp. 40-43: the de Sitter solution as exponential expansion
contents.support: The example verifies the exponential datum directly in the Friedmann-system equations and records the Lambda < 0 obstruction.

canonical.name: The flat static matter datum with constant positive density and vanishing pressure does not satisfy the Friedmann equation
canonical.support: The counterexample computes H = 0 against a strictly positive right-hand side and shows in addition that the spatial and continuity equations hold, separating the reduced equations.
